The setter should validate the correctness of the keys, the tuple format, the hour ranges and that the time blocks within a single day do not overlap. Add a read-only property total_hours.
Create a class Document with private attributes __title (str, 1–200 characters), __authors (a list of non-empty strings, at least 1 author), __metadata (a str→str dictionary) and __version (a str in semantic format, e.g. “1.2.3”). Add properties with full validation for each attribute. The version setter should additionally check whether the new version is higher than the current one. Add a read-only property summary that returns a formatted string containing the title, the authors and the version.

title: 19  Inheritance and Polymorphism
text:
Create a class Animal with an attribute name and a method speak() that returns a generic message. Then create a class Dog that inherits from Animal and overrides the speak() method so that it returns a dog’s sound.
Define a class Shape with a method area() that returns 0. Create classes Rectangle and Circle that inherit from Shape and implement their own versions of area() with the appropriate calculations.
Write a class Vehicle with attributes brand and max_speed and a method describe(). Create a class ElectricCar inheriting from Vehicle that adds an attribute battery_capacity and extends the describe() method with information about the battery.
Create a class Employee with attributes name and salary and a method get_bonus() that returns 10% of the salary. Create a class Manager inheriting from Employee in which get_bonus() returns 20% of the salary. Demonstrate the use of both classes in a single list and iterate over it.
Define a class Logger with a method log(message). Create classes FileLogger and ConsoleLogger that inherit from Logger and override log() so that they print the message with an appropriate prefix indicating where it is written. Write a function process(logger) that takes any object of type Logger and calls log() on it.
Create a class BankAccount with methods deposit(amount), withdraw(amount) and get_balance(). Then create a class SavingsAccount that inherits from BankAccount but overrides withdraw() so that it does not allow a withdrawal if the balance would drop below a set minimum.
Write a class Notification with a method send(recipient, text). Create three derived classes: EmailNotification, SmsNotification and PushNotification, each of which overrides send() and prints a message appropriate for the given channel. Write a function broadcast(notifications, recipient, text) that iterates over a list of notifications and sends them polymorphically.
Define a class Converter with a method convert(value) that returns the value unchanged. Create classes CelsiusToFahrenheit and KilometersToMiles inheriting from Converter that override convert() with the proper formulas. Use the isinstance() function to check the type of an object before conversion.
Create a class hierarchy: Media (with an attribute title), and inheriting from it Book (with author and pages), Movie (with director and duration) and Podcast (with host and episodes). Each class should have a method info() that returns a description. Write a function that takes a list of Media objects and prints information about each of them.
Create a class PaymentMethod with a method pay(amount). Create classes CreditCard, PayPal and BankTransfer that inherit from PaymentMethod. Each class should override pay() and additionally implement a method validate() that checks the correctness of the data. In the CreditCard class, use super() to call the base version of pay() before adding its own logic.
Write a class TaskRunner with methods setup(), execute() and teardown() and a method run() that calls these three methods in order. Create classes DatabaseTask and ApiTask that inherit from TaskRunner and override setup(), execute() and teardown() with their own implementations, but do not change the run() method — this is an example of the Template Method pattern.
Define a class User with attributes username and role and a method permissions() that returns an empty list. Create classes Admin, Editor and Viewer inheriting from User, each of which returns a different list of permissions. Write a function check_access(user, required_permission) that checks whether a given user has the required permission, using polymorphism.
Create an abstract class Validator (using the abc module) with an abstract method validate(data). Create classes EmailValidator, PhoneValidator and AgeValidator that implement validate() and return True or False depending on the correctness of the data. Write a function run_validations(validators, data) that runs all validators and collects the results.
Define a class Plugin with methods activate() and process(data). Create at least three derived classes representing different plugins (e.g. UpperCasePlugin, TrimPlugin, ReplacePlugin). Write a class Pipeline that stores a list of plugins and has a method run(data) that passes the data through the successive plugins polymorphically.
Create an example of multiple inheritance: a class Flyable with a method fly(), a class Swimmable with a method swim(), and a class Duck that inherits from both. Examine the method resolution order (MRO) using Duck.__mro__ and write a short comment explaining the result.
Define a class EventEmitter with methods on(event_name, callback) and emit(event_name, *args). Create a class ChatRoom inheriting from EventEmitter that adds methods join(user), leave(user) and send_message(user, text), each of which emits the corresponding event. Then create a class ModeratedChatRoom inheriting from ChatRoom that overrides send_message() and filters out forbidden words before sending.
Create a serialization system: a class Serializer with methods serialize(obj) and deserialize(data). Create classes JsonSerializer, CsvSerializer and XmlSerializer that implement these methods. Then write a class DataStore that takes an object of type Serializer in its constructor (composition) and uses it to save and load data — compare this approach with inheritance and describe in a comment when composition is better.
Define a metaclass SingletonMeta that makes every class using it able to have only one instance. Create a class DatabaseConnection using this metaclass. Then create a class PooledDatabaseConnection inheriting from DatabaseConnection and check whether the singleton mechanism also works for the derived class. Describe the result in comments.

title: 20  Text Representations of Objects
text:
Define a class Dog with attributes name and breed. Implement the __str__ method so that it returns text in the format name (breed).
Define a class Point with attributes x and y. Implement the __repr__ method so that it returns text that allows the object to be recreated, e.g. Point(3, 5).
Define a class Book with attributes title and author. Implement both methods — __str__ and __repr__ — so that they return different representations of the same object.
Create a class Temperature with an attribute celsius. The __str__ method should return the value with its unit, e.g. 36.6°C, and __repr__ — the constructor expression Temperature(36.6).
Define a class Color with attributes r, g, b. Implement __repr__ so that it satisfies the condition eval(repr(obj)) == obj (this also requires defining __eq__).
Create a class Student with attributes first_name, last_name and grade. Implement __str__ returning a friendly description of the student, and __repr__ — an unambiguous technical representation.
Write a class Fraction with attributes numerator and denominator. The __str__ method should display the fraction in the format 3/4, and __repr__ — in the format Fraction(3, 4).
Define a class Product with attributes name and price. Put several objects of this class into a list, and then print the list using print(). Observe which method — __str__ or __repr__ — is called for the elements of the list.
Create a class Vector2D with attributes x and y. Implement __repr__ and __str__, and then check what f"{obj}", str(obj) and repr(obj) return, as well as what is shown when the object is displayed in the interactive interpreter.
Write a class LogEntry with attributes timestamp, level and message. The __str__ method should return a readable log entry, and __repr__ — a full representation with all attributes, useful for debugging.
Define a class Currency with attributes amount and code (e.g. "PLN", "USD"). Implement __str__ formatting the amount with the currency symbol, and __repr__ — with full decimal precision.
Create a class Matrix that stores a two-dimensional list of numbers. Implement __str__ so that it displays the matrix in a readable row-by-row form, and __repr__ — as a single-line constructor expression.
Define a base class Shape with a __repr__ method that automatically reads the class name from type(self).__name__. Then create derived classes Circle and Rectangle that inherit this implementation and add their own attributes.
Write a class LinkedList with nodes of type Node. Implement __repr__ for the LinkedList class so that it displays the entire contents of the list in the format LinkedList(1 -> 2 -> 3).
Create a class Person with an attribute secret_code that should not appear in the output of __str__ (shown to the user) but should be visible in __repr__ (intended for the programmer).
Define a class Config that stores a dictionary of settings. Implement __repr__, which displays the sorted keys and their values, and __str__, which displays only the number of keys and the names of the first three.
Write a class decorator auto_repr that automatically generates a __repr__ method based on the attributes passed to __init__. Test it on at least two different classes.
Create a class hierarchy Animal -> Mammal -> Cat. At each level, implement __repr__ that calls super().__repr__() and appends the attributes specific to that level. Analyze the resulting representation string.
Define a class LazyRepr in which the __repr__ method performs an expensive operation (e.g. simulated with time.sleep). Then write an optimized version that caches the result of __repr__ using the memoization technique and compare the execution times.
Write a metaclass ReprEnforcerMeta that, when a class is created, checks whether the class defines both __str__ and __repr__. If either of these methods is missing, the metaclass should raise a TypeError exception with an appropriate message.

title: 21  Container Emulation
text:
Define a class MyList that wraps a regular list. Implement the __len__ method, which returns the number of elements, and test how the built-in len() function works on an object of this class.
Create a class Sentence that stores text as a string. Implement __len__ so that it returns the number of words in the sentence rather than the number of characters.
Define a class ColorPalette that stores a list of colors. Implement __getitem__ so that colors can be retrieved by index, e.g. palette[2].
Extend the ColorPalette class with a __setitem__ method that allows replacing the color at a given index, e.g. palette[0] = "red".
Write a class Matrix that stores data in a flat list. Implement __getitem__ taking a tuple (row, col), so that element access looks like matrix[2, 3].
Create a class DefaultDict that emulates a dictionary with a default value. Implement __getitem__ so that for a non-existent key it returns the value given at initialization instead of raising a KeyError.
Define a class Scoreboard that stores player scores in a dictionary. Implement __getitem__, __setitem__ and __len__, and then test the operations board["Alice"], board["Bob"] = 10 and len(board) on it.
Write a class ImmutableList that implements __getitem__ and __len__ but deliberately does not define __setitem__. Check which exception is raised when you try to assign a value to an element.
Create a class RangeMap in which __getitem__ takes an integer and returns the name of the range that the number belongs to (e.g. 0-10 is "low", 11-20 is "medium"). The ranges are defined at initialization.
Define a class CircularBuffer with a fixed size. Implement __getitem__, __setitem__ and __len__ so that indices beyond the size of the buffer automatically wrap around cyclically.
Write a class SparseVector that stores only the non-zero elements in a dictionary. Implement __getitem__ (returning 0 for missing indices), __setitem__ (removing the key when the value is set to 0) and __len__ (returning the logical size of the vector).
Create a class History that emulates a container with the ability to undo changes. The __setitem__ method should push the previous value of the key onto a stack, and an additional method undo(key) should restore the last value.
Define a class SliceableString that implements __getitem__ with full support for slices. The expression obj[1:5] should return a new SliceableString object, and obj[0] — a single character.
Write a class Table with data in the form of a list of dictionaries. Implement __getitem__ so that it supports three access modes — by row index (int), by column name (string) and by a tuple (row_index, column_name).
Create a class ValidatedList in which __setitem__ checks the type of the inserted value and raises a TypeError if it does not match the type given at initialization (e.g. ValidatedList(int)).
Define a class NestedDict that allows access to nested data using a key in the form of a dotted path, e.g. config["database.host"] instead of config["database"]["host"]. Implement both __getitem__ and __setitem__.
Write a class TimeSeries that stores (datetime, value) pairs. Implement __getitem__ so that it accepts both a numeric index and a datetime object (looking up the nearest point in time), as well as a slice with datetime objects as the bounds of the range.
Create a class ChainMap that takes several dictionaries in its constructor. Implement __getitem__ searching the dictionaries in order, __setitem__ always writing to the first dictionary, and __len__ returning the number of unique keys across all dictionaries.
Define a class DatabaseTable that emulates a database table. Implement __getitem__ supporting queries in the style of table[lambda row: row["age"] > 18], returning a new DatabaseTable object with the filtered rows. Add __len__ and __setitem__ for updating the rows that satisfy a condition.
Write a class TensorView that wraps a one-dimensional list of data and interprets it as a tensor of a given shape (e.g. (2, 3, 4)). Implement __getitem__ with support for multidimensional indexing and slicing along each dimension, __setitem__ with analogous logic, and __len__ returning the size of the first dimension. Make sure that the view shares data with the original.

title: 22  Arithmetic Emulation
text:
Write a class Temperature with an attribute celsius. Implement the __add__ method, which makes it possible to add two Temperature objects — the result should be a new object with the sum of the values.
Write a class Counter that stores an integer. Implement the __add__ and __sub__ methods so that Counter objects can be added to and subtracted from each other using the + and - operators.
Write a class Vector2D with attributes x and y. Implement the __mul__ method, which allows multiplying a vector by a scalar (a number), returning a new vector with scaled coordinates.
Write a class Price that stores an amount as a float. Implement the __truediv__ method so that the / operator divides the price by a given number and returns a new Price object.
Write a class Weight with an attribute kg. Implement the __add__ and __sub__ methods with support for adding/subtracting both another Weight object and a plain number (a scalar).
Write a class Wallet with an attribute balance. Implement __floordiv__ (the // operator), which performs integer division of the balance by a given number, and __mod__ (the % operator), which returns the remainder of the division.
Write a class DataSeries that stores a list of numeric values. Implement __add__, which performs element-by-element (elementwise) addition of two DataSeries objects of the same length. If the lengths do not match, raise a ValueError.
Write a class Score with an attribute points. Implement __radd__ so that the expression 10 + score_obj correctly delegates the operation to the Score object — test that both score + 10 and 10 + score work.
Write a class Matrix1D that stores a one-dimensional list of values. Implement __mul__ handling two scenarios: multiplication by a scalar and the element-by-element product with another Matrix1D object. Add __rmul__ for expressions such as 3 * matrix_obj.
Write a class Measurement with attributes value and unit. Implement __add__ and __sub__, which allow combining only measurements with the same unit — if the units do not match, raise a TypeError with a message describing the conflict.
Write a class Percentage with an attribute value (e.g. 75 means 75%). Implement __mul__ so that Percentage(50) * 200 returns a float equal to 100.0 (calculating a percentage of a number), and multiplying two Percentage objects returns a new Percentage object with the compound percentage.
Write a class BankAccount with an attribute balance. Implement __iadd__ and __isub__ (the += and -= operators) so that they modify the balance in place. In the case of __isub__, prevent the balance from going below zero by raising a ValueError.
Write a class ComplexNumber with attributes real and imag. Implement the __add__, __sub__ and __mul__ methods according to the rules of complex number arithmetic. Also implement __repr__ so that the result is displayed in the format a + bi.
Write a class Polynomial that represents a polynomial as a list of coefficients (the list index corresponds to the power). Implement __add__ (adding polynomials) and __mul__ (multiplying polynomials by a scalar). Pay attention to polynomials of different degrees.
Write a class TimeDelta with an attribute seconds. Implement __add__, __sub__, __mul__ (multiplication by a scalar) and __truediv__. The / operator should distinguish division by a number (returns a TimeDelta) from division by another TimeDelta (returns a float — the ratio of the durations).
Write a class Vector3D with attributes x, y, z. Implement __add__, __sub__, __mul__ (the dot product with another vector returning a float, or scaling the vector by a number), __rmul__ and __neg__ (the unary - operator). Use type hinting and isinstance to distinguish between operand types.
Write a class Currency with attributes amount and code (e.g. “PLN”, “USD”). Implement __add__, __sub__, __mul__ (by a scalar) and __truediv__ (by a scalar). Addition and subtraction between different currencies should be forbidden (raise a TypeError). Add the __radd__ and __rmul__ methods for commutativity with scalars.
Write a class FractionNumber with attributes numerator and denominator. Implement __add__, __sub__, __mul__ and __truediv__ with full fraction arithmetic (including bringing fractions to a common denominator). Each operation should return the fraction in reduced form — use math.gcd to simplify the result.
Write a class SparseVector that stores a sparse vector as a dictionary (the keys are the indices of the non-zero elements). Implement __add__, __sub__ and __mul__ (the dot product with another SparseVector returning a float, or scaling by a number). Make sure the keys are merged correctly and zeros are removed from the resulting dictionary.
Write a family of classes representing physical units: Distance (meters), Time (seconds) and Speed (meters per second). Implement the arithmetic operators so that Distance / Time returns Speed and Speed * Time returns Distance. Also handle adding and subtracting objects of the same type and multiplication by a scalar. For invalid operations (e.g. Distance + Time), raise a TypeError.

title: 23  Comparison Emulation
text:
Write a class Temperature with a degrees attribute. Implement the __eq__ method, which compares two objects of this class based on the value of degrees. Test the == operator on two instances.
In a class Product with attributes name and price, implement the __lt__ method so that the < operator compares products by price. Create three objects and check the result of the comparison.
Extend the Product class from the previous task with the __le__ method. Make sure the method correctly handles the case where the prices are equal.
Write a class Student with attributes name and grade. Implement the __eq__ and __lt__ methods, then sort a list of students using the built-in sorted() function.
In a class DataPoint with attributes label and value, implement the __eq__ method so that it returns NotImplemented when other is not an instance of DataPoint. Explain in a comment why we return NotImplemented instead of False.
Write a class Rectangle with attributes width and height. Implement the __eq__, __lt__ and __gt__ methods so that comparisons are based on the area of the rectangle.
Use the @functools.total_ordering decorator in a class Score with a points attribute. Define only __eq__ and __lt__, then test all six comparison operators (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=).
Write a class SemanticVersion with attributes major, minor and patch. Implement the __eq__ and __lt__ methods so that they compare versions lexicographically (first major, then minor, then patch). Sort a list of versions.
In a class Interval with attributes start and end, implement the __eq__ method comparing both endpoints of the interval and __lt__ comparing intervals by their length. Check that two intervals with different endpoints but the same length are not equal.
Write a class Employee with attributes name, department and salary. Implement __eq__ comparing by name and department (without salary) and __lt__ comparing by salary only. In a comment, consider the consequences of such an inconsistent definition of equality and ordering.
Write a class Vector2D with attributes x and y. Implement __eq__ comparing both components. Then define __lt__ comparing vectors by their Euclidean length. Add type hints to all methods.
In a class Exam with attributes subject and score, implement __eq__ and __lt__. Then create a list of Exam objects and find its maximum element using the built-in max() function — without passing the key parameter.
Write a class TemperatureReading with a celsius attribute. Implement the __eq__ and __lt__ methods, which compare temperatures with a given tolerance epsilon (e.g. 0.01). Two temperatures that differ by less than epsilon should be considered equal.
Create a class Money with attributes amount and currency. Implement __eq__ and __lt__ so that they raise a ValueError exception when we try to compare amounts in different currencies. Test both scenarios — matching and mismatching currencies.
Write a class Card with attributes rank and suit, representing a playing card. Define a dictionary with the order of ranks (e.g. “2” to “A”) and implement __eq__ and __lt__ taking this order into account. Use @total_ordering. Sort a deck of five cards.
In a class TimeSeries storing a list of values, implement __eq__, which compares series element by element, and __lt__, which compares series by their arithmetic mean. Handle the case of series of different lengths in __eq__ (they should be unequal).
Write a class Matrix2x2 storing a 2x2 matrix as a list of lists. Implement __eq__ comparing element by element. Define __lt__ comparing matrices by their determinants. Add a __repr__ method that displays the matrix in a readable way.
Create a class hierarchy: a base class Shape and derived classes Circle and Square. In the Shape class, define the abstract method area(). Implement __eq__ and __lt__ in the Shape class, comparing by area(). Check that comparing a Circle with a Square works correctly thanks to inheritance.
Write a class CacheEntry with attributes key, value and priority. Implement __eq__ comparing by key and __lt__ comparing by priority. Then use the heapq module to build a priority queue based on CacheEntry objects — heapq requires a correctly defined < operator.
Write a (simplified) class DataFrame storing a dictionary of columns (name -> list of values). Implement __eq__ checking the equality of structure and data column by column. Define __lt__ comparing frames by the number of rows. Additionally, implement __hash__ so that DataFrame objects are unhashable (as in pandas) — assign __hash__ = None — and explain in a comment why changing __eq__ requires careful consideration of __hash__.

title: 24  Decorators
text:
In addition to defining each decorator, use it at least once.

Write a decorator call_counter that counts how many times a given function has been called. Store the counter as an attribute of the wrapper function. After each call, print the current value of the counter to the console.
Write a decorator log_call that prints the function’s name before calling it and prints the returned value after the call. Use the __name__ attribute of the original function.
Write a decorator timer that measures the function’s execution time in seconds (the time module) and prints it when the function finishes. Return the result of the original function unchanged.
Write a decorator suppress_errors that catches all exceptions raised by the function, prints a message with the error text and returns None instead of propagating the exception.
Write a decorator repeat(n) that takes an argument n and causes the decorated function to be called n times with the same arguments. The decorator returns the result of the last call.
Write a decorator cache_result that stores the results of function calls in a dictionary, using the positional arguments as the key. If the function has already been called with the same arguments, return the result from the dictionary without calling it again.
Write a decorator validate_types that takes types as positional arguments (e.g. @validate_types(int, int)). Before calling the function, check whether the passed arguments have the corresponding types. If not, raise TypeError with a descriptive message.
Write a decorator retry(max_attempts, delay) that, when an exception occurs, retries the function call up to max_attempts times, waiting delay seconds between attempts. If all attempts fail, raise the last exception.
Write a decorator flatten_result that, after calling the function, checks whether the result is a nested list (a list of lists). If so, it flattens it into a single-level list. If the result is not a list, it returns it unchanged.
Write a decorator sort_result(key=None, reverse=False) that sorts the function’s result if it is a list. The key and reverse parameters work the same way as in the built-in sorted function. If the result is not a list, return it unchanged.
Write a decorator transform_keys(func) that takes a transforming function (e.g. str.upper). If the decorated function returns a dictionary, apply the transformation to all keys of that dictionary. If the result is not a dictionary, return it unchanged.
Write a decorator ensure_keys(*required_keys) that checks whether the dictionary returned by the decorated function contains all the required keys. If any key is missing, raise KeyError with a list of the missing keys. If the result is not a dictionary, raise TypeError.
Write a decorator paginate(page_size) that takes a page size. If the decorated function returns a list, the decorator turns it into a list of sublists, each of which has at most page_size elements. If the result is not a list, return it unchanged.
Write a decorator filter_result(predicate) that takes a filtering function. If the decorated function returns a list, the decorator keeps only those elements for which predicate returns True. If the result is not a list, return it unchanged.
Write a decorator default_args(**defaults) that takes default values for keyword arguments. If the decorated function is called without any of these arguments, the decorator adds it automatically. Use the inspect module to examine the function’s signature.
Write a decorator audit_log(log_list) that takes an external list as an argument. After each call of the decorated function, it appends to this list a dictionary containing the keys: function_name, args, kwargs, result and timestamp (use datetime.datetime.now()).
Write a decorator compose(*decorators) that takes any number of other decorators and applies them in turn to the decorated function (the first decorator in the list wraps the function first, the last one last). Test it by combining at least two of the decorators written earlier.
Write a decorator rate_limit(max_calls, period) that allows at most max_calls calls of the decorated function within period seconds. If the limit is exceeded, raise a RuntimeError exception with information on how many seconds remain until it is unblocked.
Write a decorator dispatch_on_type that registers different implementations of a function depending on the type of the first argument. The decorator exposes a register(type, func) method on the wrapper function. When called, it checks the type of the first argument and delegates to the appropriate registered implementation. If the type is not registered, it calls the default function.
Write a decorator pipeline(*transformers) that takes any number of transforming functions. After calling the decorated function, it passes its result through each transformer in turn. If any transformer raises an exception, stop the chain, print a diagnostic message indicating which transformer failed, and return the result from before that step.

title: 25  Regular Expressions
text:
Import the re module and use re.findall() to find all floating-point numbers in the text "Price: 49.99 PLN, discount: 10.50 PLN", using the pattern r"\d+\.\d+".
Explain the difference between writing the pattern as "\\d+\\.\\d+" and as r"\d+\.\d+". Which one is more readable and why?
Given the string text = "Report_2024 report_2025 REPORT_2026", use re.findall() with a pattern containing \d{4} to extract all four-digit numbers from it.
Given the string log = "ERROR: file not found at /data/input.csv", write a pattern with r"\b...\b" that searches it for exactly the word file as a whole word (not as part of another word).
Given the list files = ["data.csv", "report.pdf", "sales.xlsx", "model.pkl"], write an expression with re.search() and a pattern using the alternation (csv|xlsx) and the anchor $ that filters out only the files with the csv or xlsx extension.
Given the string record = "  John Smith  (b. 1990) " (b. is the abbreviation for “born”), use re.sub() with an appropriate pattern in an r-string to remove the parenthesized fragment containing the year of birth.
Given the string messy = "Anna   BROWN   (b.  1985)", apply re.sub(r"\s+", " ", messy) to replace multiple whitespace characters with a single space. Describe what the + quantifier does here.
Write a regular expression in an r-string that matches an optional dot after the abbreviation b (for “born”) — use the ? quantifier in the pattern r"\bb\.?".
Define the variable column = "price" and use an rf-string to create the pattern rf"\b{column}\b". Then use re.findall() on the text "The total_price and price are different" and explain why the result contains only "price".
Given the list of extensions extensions = ["csv", "xlsx", "parquet"], dynamically build a regex pattern using an rf-string and the join() method so that the resulting pattern is r"\.(csv|xlsx|parquet)$".
Given the string data = "Height: 180cm, weight: 75kg, age: 30yrs", write a pattern with re.findall() that extracts all numbers (sequences of digits), using r"\d+".
Given the list of records raw_data = ["John Smith (b. 1990)", "Anna Brown (b. 1985)"], write a for loop in which you use re.sub() to remove the fragment with the year of birth and then remove redundant spaces — as in the lecture example.
Write a pattern in an r-string that matches any sequence of whitespace characters (\s+) surrounded by word boundaries (\b). Test it on the string "Hello   World" using re.sub(), replacing multiple spaces with a hyphen.
Given the string line = "error: timeout at 12:45:30", use re.search() with the pattern r"\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}" to find the timestamp in it. Explain the role of the {2} quantifier in the pattern.
Given the list of files all_files = ["notes.txt", "data.csv", "image.png", "report.xlsx", "archive.parquet"], write a list comprehension with re.search() and a dynamically built rf-pattern (based on a list of extensions) that returns only the data files.
Given the text info = "PETER   Wilson(b.2000)", apply two re.sub() operations to it in turn: the first to remove the fragment with the year of birth (note the absence of a space before the parenthesis), the second to normalize the spaces. Finally, call .strip().title().
Write a pattern in an r-string that matches e-mail addresses in a simplified form: a sequence of alphanumeric characters, the @ sign, a sequence of alphanumeric characters, a dot and a domain. Use \w+, a literal dot \. and re.findall().
Define a list of banned words banned = ["error", "fail", "crash"]. Using an rf-string and the join() method, create a pattern with alternation and word boundaries \b, then use re.findall() to search for these words in a sample log.
Given a multiline string with data in the format "key: value", write a pattern with re.findall() using a group () and \s+ that extracts only the values (after the colon and space). Use an r-string.
Write a function clean_records(records) that takes a list of strings in the format "FIRSTNAME LASTNAME (b. YYYY)". Using re.sub() with an r-string, the function should remove the year of birth in parentheses, normalize the spaces (\s+), trim the string (.strip()) and apply .title(). Return the list of cleaned records. Use an rf-string so that the pattern handles an optional space and an optional dot after b.

title: 26  Iterators and Generators
text:
Write a class CountdownIterator that takes an integer start and, when iterated over, returns successive numbers from start down to 0 inclusive. Use the iterator protocol (__iter__, __next__).
Create a generator expression cubes that produces the cubes of successive numbers for range(20). Then use sum() to calculate their sum.
Implement a class RangeIterator with parameters start, stop and step that works analogously to the built-in range, but fully uses the iterator protocol.
Write a generator function even_numbers(limit) that returns successive even numbers less than limit. Use it in a for loop to print the values.
Using a list comprehension, transform the list raw_data = ["12", "abc", "7.5", "", "3", "xyz"] into a list of integers containing only the valid integer values.
Write a class FibonacciIterator that returns the next number of the Fibonacci sequence on each call of __next__(). The iterator should stop after generating n elements (StopIteration).
Create a generator function chunked(data, chunk_size) that works similarly to the DataBatchIterator class from the lecture, but uses the yield statement instead of a class.
Write a dictionary comprehension word_lengths that, for the list words = ["python", "data", "iterator", "yield", "set"], returns a mapping word → its length, but only for words longer than 3 characters.
Implement a generator running_average(numbers) that, for a list of numbers, returns successive values of the running average (after the first, second, third… element).
Write a class ReverseIterator that takes a sequence and, when iterated over, returns its elements in reverse order. Do not use the reversed() function.
Create a generator pipeline for the list of strings lines = ["10", "abc", "20", "", "30"]: the first generator filters the values that are numbers, the second converts them to int, the third squares them. Calculate the final sum using sum().
Write a generator function cycle_n_times(iterable, n) that iterates over the given iterable n times, returning successive elements.
Using a generator expression and the any() function, check whether the list numbers = [3, 7, 11, 14, 19, 25] contains any number divisible by 5. Then use all() to check whether all of them are less than 30.
Implement a class BatchIterator with type hinting (use Iterator, List, Any from the typing module) that returns data in batches of a given size, but additionally skips batches containing fewer than min_size elements.
Create a set comprehension unique_first_letters containing the first letters (lowercase) of the words from the list words = ["Apple", "banana", "apricot", "Cherry", "blueberry"], but only for words at least 5 characters long.
Write a generator function read_lines_filtered(filepath, keyword) that reads a file line by line and returns only those lines that contain the given keyword (after strip()). Use the with open(...) statement.
Implement a class ZipIterator that takes two sequences and, when iterated over, returns tuples of pairs of corresponding elements. Iteration ends when the shorter of the sequences is exhausted. Do not use the built-in zip().
Write a generator pipeline for processing a CSV file (analogous to the lecture example): load_records reads the rows, filter_valid rejects records with a missing value in column 1, extract_feature returns numeric values from a selected column. Then write a function compute_stats(pipeline) that returns a dictionary with the keys min, max, mean. Use type hinting (Generator, List, Dict).
Using a nested list comprehension, generate a 5×5 multiplication table as a list of lists. Then use a generator expression to calculate the sum of all elements on the diagonal.
Implement a class MovingWindowIterator with type hinting that takes a sequence data: List[Any] and window_size: int. When iterated over, it returns successive sublists (windows) of the given size, shifted by one element. Once all possible windows are exhausted, it raises StopIteration. Additionally, write a generator expression that uses this class to calculate the mean in each window for a list of numbers.

title: 27  Bitwise Operators
text:
Write a function is_even that takes an integer and returns a Boolean value. Using the & operator, the function should check whether the number is even. The function should also work correctly for negative numbers.
Write a function last_bit that takes an integer and returns the value of its least significant bit (0 or 1).
Write a function multiply_by_power_of_two that takes two integers x and n and returns the result of multiplying x by 2^n using a bit shift. Then write an analogous function divide_by_power_of_two that performs integer division.
Write a function mod_power_of_two that takes two integers x and n and returns the remainder of dividing x by 2^n, using only bitwise operators (without %).
Write a function get_bit that takes an integer x and a position i (an integer) and returns the value of the bit at position i in the number x (counting from position 0 as the least significant).
Write three functions: set_bit, clear_bit and toggle_bit. Each of them takes an integer x and a position i (an integer) and returns an integer — with the bit at position i set, cleared and toggled, respectively.
Write a function to_u2 that takes an integer x and a number of bits bits (an integer) and returns the two’s complement (U2) representation of x at the given width as a string of zeros and ones.
Write a function count_ones that takes a non-negative integer and returns an integer equal to the number of bits set to 1. Use the bin function and the count method.
Write a function hamming_distance that takes two integers and returns an integer equal to the Hamming distance between them (the number of positions at which their bits differ).
Write a function is_power_of_two that takes an integer and returns a Boolean value indicating whether this number is a positive power of two. Use the x & (x - 1) pattern.
Write a function lowest_set_bit that takes an integer x and returns an integer equal to the value of the lowest set bit (e.g. for the input 44 it returns 4). Use an expression with -x.
Write a function find_unique that takes a list of integers and returns an integer — the only value that appears an odd number of times, when all the others occur in pairs. Use XOR and a for loop.
Write a function xor_swap that takes two integers a and b and returns a tuple of two integers with the values swapped. Do not use a temporary variable — use only the ^ operator.
Write a function reverse_bits that takes an integer x and a number of bits bits (an integer) and returns the integer obtained by reversing the order of bits in the bits-bit representation of x (e.g. for x = 0b1011 and bits = 4 the result is 0b1101).
Write a function extract_byte that takes an integer x and a byte number n (an integer) and returns an integer equal to the value of the n-th byte of x (byte zero is the least significant 8 bits). Use a combination of >> and the mask & 0xFF.
Define a set of permission flags using IntFlag and auto: READ, WRITE, EXECUTE, ADMIN. Write three functions: grant, which takes the current permissions and a new flag and returns the new permissions; revoke, which takes the current permissions and a flag to remove and returns the new permissions; and has_all, which takes the current permissions and the required flags and returns a Boolean value indicating whether the current permissions contain all the required flags.
Write a class Bitmask with fields value (an integer) and width (an integer) and the methods: set (takes a bit position, returns nothing), clear (takes a bit position, returns nothing), flip (takes a bit position, returns nothing), is_set (takes a bit position, returns a Boolean value) and __repr__, which returns a binary representation of width width padded with leading zeros.
Extend the BitSet class from the lecture with a difference method, which takes another BitSet object and returns a new BitSet containing the elements present in self but absent from other. Also add an is_subset method, which takes another BitSet object and returns a Boolean value indicating whether self is a subset of other.
Write a class BloomFilter with the methods: __init__, which takes a size (an integer) and returns nothing; add, which takes a value (an integer) and returns nothing; and __contains__, which takes a value (an integer) and returns a Boolean value. The filter should store its data in a single field bits (an integer) and use three simple hash functions of the form (value * k) & (size - 1) for k = 1, 3, 7. The add method sets the corresponding bits, and the in operator checks whether all these bits are set. Assume that the size is a power of two.
Write a class Xorshift32 implementing a pseudorandom number generator from the xorshift family. In the __init__ method (takes a seed that is an integer, returns nothing), store the seed in the field state (an integer). The next method (takes no arguments, returns an integer) should perform, in order: state ^= (state << 13) & 0xFFFFFFFF, state ^= (state >> 17), state ^= (state << 5) & 0xFFFFFFFF, and then return the new value of the state field masked to 32 bits. Add a random_below method, which takes an integer n and returns an integer in the range [0, n), assuming that n is a power of two.

title: 28  Selected Sequence Types
text:
Write a function to_bytes_literal that takes an ASCII string and returns the corresponding bytes object written as a literal with the b prefix. Then print the type of the result and its length.
Write a function count_byte that takes a bytes object and a single byte (an integer in the range 0–255) and returns an integer equal to the number of occurrences of that byte in the sequence.
Write a function pack_three_doubles that takes three floating-point numbers and returns a bytes object produced by serializing them with struct.pack using the format "3d". Check the length of the result and make sure it is 24.
Write a function unpack_three_doubles that takes a bytes object of length 24 and returns a tuple of three floating-point numbers recovered using struct.unpack.
Write a function pack_vector that takes a list of floating-point numbers of any length and returns a bytes object with their serialization in the format f"{len(values)}d". Then write a function unpack_vector that takes a bytes object and the number of elements (an integer) and returns a tuple of floating-point numbers.
Write a function to_mutable that takes a bytes object and returns the corresponding bytearray object. Also write a function to_immutable that performs the conversion in the other direction.
Write a function replace_first_byte that takes a bytearray object and a new byte value (an integer in the range 0–255), changes the first byte to the given value and returns nothing. The function should modify the buffer in place.
Write a function overwrite_double that takes a bytearray object containing a serialized vector of floating-point numbers, an element index (an integer) and a new value (a floating-point number), and overwrites the indicated element using struct.pack_into with the format "d". The function returns nothing.
Write a function build_int_array that takes a list of integers and returns an array.array object with type code 'i' (int32) containing these values.
Write a function array_memory_usage that takes an array.array object and returns an integer equal to the estimated size of the memory it occupies in bytes. Use buffer_info and the itemsize field.
Write a function compare_memory that takes an integer n, creates a regular list list(range(n)) and an array.array with type code 'i' containing the same elements, and then prints the memory size of both structures. For the list use sys.getsizeof; for the array use the product of the length and itemsize.
Write a function save_floats that takes an array.array object with type code 'd' and a file path (a string), and then writes the contents of the array to a binary file using tofile. The function returns nothing.
Write a function load_floats that takes a file path (a string) and the number of elements to read (an integer) and returns an array.array object with type code 'd' loaded from a binary file using fromfile.
Write a function roundtrip_array that takes a list of floating-point numbers and a file path (a string). The function should create an array.array with type code 'd', write it to the file, read it back from the file and return the array that was read.
Write a function array_from_generator that takes an integer n and returns an array.array object with type code 'd' containing n values of the form x * 0.1 for x ranging from 0 to n-1. Use a generator expression passed to the array.array constructor.
Write a function read_pgm_header that takes the path to a PGM file (a string) and returns a tuple containing the width, height and maximum pixel value (three integers). The function should open the file in "rb" mode, read the line with the magic number b"P5", skip comment lines beginning with b"#" and not read the pixels themselves.
Write a function read_pgm_pixels that takes the path to a PGM file (a string) and returns a tuple: width (an integer), height (an integer), maximum value (an integer) and a bytearray object with the raw pixels. The function should verify the magic number b"P5" using an assert statement.
Write a function pixels_to_matrix that takes a bytearray object with the pixels of an image, the width (an integer) and the height (an integer), and returns a list of lists of integers representing the image row by row. Use sequence slicing and the list constructor.
Write a function invert_pgm that takes a bytearray object with the pixels of a PGM image and the maximum pixel value (an integer), modifies the buffer in place so that each pixel is replaced with the value max_val - pixel (the negative of the image), and returns nothing. Use a for loop over the indices.
Write a function pgm_pipeline that takes the path to an input PGM file (a string) and the path to an output file (a string). The function should read the header and pixels of the image (analogously to read_pgm_pixels), store the pixels in an array.array with type code 'b' or 'B', write this array to a binary file using tofile, and then read it back using fromfile and return the array that was read.

title: 29  Lambda Expressions
text:
Write a lambda expression named cube that takes an integer and returns its cube. Call it for the value 4 and print the result.
Define a lambda expression area_rectangle that takes two arguments (length and width) and returns the area of the rectangle. Check how it works for several pairs of values.
Using the map function and a lambda expression, transform the list of integers numbers into a list of their absolute values. Print the result as a list.
Using filter and a lambda expression, select from the list words only those strings whose length is greater than 5. The result should be a new list.
Sort the list of tuples points of the form (x, y) in ascending order by the second coordinate, using the sorted function and the key parameter given as a lambda expression.
Given a list of dictionaries students, in which each element contains the keys name and grade, sort it in descending order by the value of grade using sorted and a lambda.
Using functools.reduce and a lambda expression, calculate the sum of squares of the elements of the list values containing floating-point numbers.
Using reduce and a lambda, find the largest element in the list of integers numbers without using the built-in max function.
Define a lambda expression classify_temperature that, for a given temperature (a floating-point number), returns one of the strings "cold", "warm" or "hot", depending on the range (below 10, between 10 and 25, above 25). Use a conditional expression.
For a list of strings names, use a combination of map and a lambda to convert each name to a format in which the first letter is uppercase and the rest are lowercase. Then, from the transformed list, filter out the names beginning with the letter A.
Given two lists of equal length — prices and quantities — use zip, map and a lambda to calculate a list of the products of corresponding elements.
Using enumerate and a lambda expression passed to map, create a list of strings of the form "i: value" for each position of the list items.
Write a generator expression even_squares that, for successive numbers in the range from 1 to 100, returns the squares of the even numbers. Then print the first five values using next.
Using the iter and next functions, manually retrieve the first three elements of the list letters containing letters of the alphabet. Explain in a comment the difference between an iterable and an iterator.
Define a function make_multiplier that takes a number factor and returns a lambda expression that multiplies its argument by this number. Demonstrate how it works by creating the functions double and triple.
Given a list of words text_tokens, use sorted together with a lambda to order them first in ascending order by word length and then alphabetically (use a tuple as the value returned by the key).
Using only map, filter and lambdas, write an expression that calculates the sum of cubes of the odd numbers in the range from 1 to 50. Use the sum function for the final summation.
Implement a generator function running_average that, for a given iterable of numbers, returns successive running averages. Then, using map and a lambda, round the results to two decimal places.
Given a list of dictionaries transactions with the keys category and amount, use reduce and a lambda to calculate a dictionary aggregating the sums of amounts within each category. The accumulator should be an empty dictionary.
Write a function compose that takes any number of single-argument functions (passed as lambda expressions) and returns their composition as a single lambda expression. Demonstrate how it works by composing three operations: adding 1, squaring and multiplying by 2.

title: 30  The functools Module
text:
Using functools.reduce, calculate the sum of the elements of the list of integers values. Set the initial value of the accumulator to 0.
Using functools.reduce and the operator module, calculate the product of the elements of the list numbers containing floating-point numbers. Do not use a lambda expression.
Write a function clip_value that takes a value, a lower limit and an upper limit and returns the value clipped to the given range. Then, using functools.partial, create a function clip_percent with the limits set to 0 and 100.
Define a function format_number(value, precision, suffix) that returns a formatted string. Using functools.partial, configure a variant format_percent with precision 2 and the suffix "%" and a variant format_currency with precision 2 and the suffix " PLN".
Using the functools.lru_cache decorator, recursively implement a function fibonacci(n) that returns the n-th term of the Fibonacci sequence. Call the function for the value 100 and print the result.
Implement a recursive function binomial(n, k) that calculates the binomial coefficient. Use the functools.cache decorator, and then, after several calls, print the statistics from cache_info.
Using the functools.lru_cache(maxsize=32) decorator, implement a function expensive_lookup(key) that simulates an expensive data fetch by calling time.sleep(1) and returning a dictionary. Measure the time of the second call with the same argument and compare it with the first.
Explain in a comment why a function decorated with lru_cache will not work if we pass it an argument of type list. Then write a function sum_unique(items) that takes a tuple and returns the sum of its unique values, and demonstrate the use of the cache with different tuples as input.
Define a class Statistics with a constructor that takes a sequence of numbers. Use functools.cached_property to define the attributes mean, variance and stdev. Inside each method, add a print call reporting that the computation has started, in order to verify that it is performed only once.
Implement a class TextAnalyzer with a constructor that takes a string. Using functools.cached_property, add the attributes word_count, unique_words (returning a set) and most_common (returning the most frequently occurring word).
Using functools.singledispatch, define a function describe(value) that returns the string "integer: ..." for an argument of type int, the string "float: ..." for float, and the string "string of length ..." for str. Add a default implementation that raises TypeError.
Using functools.singledispatch, write a function serialize(data) that, for a list, returns its representation as a string with the elements separated by commas; for a dictionary, as key=value pairs separated by semicolons; and for a tuple, as the elements in round brackets.
Write a decorator log_calls that prints the name of the decorated function and the passed arguments before each call. Use functools.wraps to preserve the metadata of the original function. Check that __name__ and __doc__ of the decorated function are preserved.
Implement a decorator retry(times) that retries the function call up to times times if an exception is raised. Use functools.wraps. Test the decorator on a function that randomly either raises an exception or returns a result.
Using the functools.total_ordering decorator, implement a class Temperature that stores a value in degrees Celsius. Define only the __eq__ and __lt__ methods, and then check how all the comparison operators and the sorted function work on a list of instances.
Using functools.total_ordering, implement a class Version whose instances are compared based on the tuple (major, minor, patch). Demonstrate the use of the <, >= and == operators and the sorting of a list of objects.
Using functools.reduce and the operator.and_ function from the operator module, calculate the intersection of the list of sets sets_list. Then do the same for the union of the sets, using operator.or_.
Given a list of dictionaries records, in which each element contains the keys category and amount, use functools.reduce to build a dictionary aggregating the sums of amounts per category. The accumulator should be an empty dictionary.
Write a decorator memoize_with_stats that combines memoization with a hit and miss counter (without using lru_cache). Use functools.wraps. The decorator should add the methods cache_hits and cache_misses to the function, returning the current counters.
Using functools.partial, functools.reduce and functools.singledispatch, design a function pipeline(value, *steps) that applies a sequence of transformations to the input value. Then define a singledispatch function apply_default that provides different transformation steps for the types int, str and list, and use partial to configure reusable variants of the pipeline steps.
